issues.legal_issue: A donor who continues to occupy gifted property is not entirely excluded from its possession and enjoyment merely because the donor has no enforceable right to remain there.
material_facts: The parents gifted the house to their two sons, and the gift document recited that the sons had accepted the gift and been put in possession.
The sons paid the municipal tax after the gift, but the parents continued to live in the house and the father continued to look after its affairs as head of the family until his death.
The father’s continued residence was not based on an enforceable right; the sons permitted it through filial affection.
issues.conclusion: The donor was not entirely excluded from possession and enjoyment of the house, so it was deemed to pass on his death and was liable to estate duty.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953 requires cumulatively that the donee bona fide assume possession and enjoyment to the exclusion of the donor immediately upon the gift, and retain it thereafter to the entire exclusion of the donor and of any benefit to the donor. The first condition is not satisfied where the donor continues to occupy or enjoy the property, even without an enforceable right to do so. The Court relied on Attorney-General v. Earl Grey and Chick v. Commissioner of Stamp Duties of New South Wales, and considered Commissioner of Stamp Duties of New South Wales v. Owens; it declined to follow Attorney-General v. Seccombe on the need for an enforceable right to establish non-exclusion. Section 5 imposes estate duty on the estate of a person dying after the Act commenced.

rule.if: estate_duty_gift_proceeding and gift_made and (not donee_immediately_assumed_exclusive_possession or not donee_thereafter_retained_exclusive_possession)

predicates.estate_duty_gift_proceeding: The matter is an estate-duty proceeding concerning property transferred by gift.
predicates.gift_made: The donor transferred the property to a donee by gift.
predicates.donee_immediately_assumed_exclusive_poss: The donee bona fide took possession and enjoyment of the gifted property immediately, excluding the donor.
predicates.donee_thereafter_retained_exclusive_poss: The donee thereafter retained possession and enjoyment of the gifted property to the entire exclusion of the donor and any benefit to the donor.
predicates.gifted_property_is_deemed_to_pass_on_don: The gifted property is treated as passing on the donor’s death for estate-duty purposes.

issues.definition: In an estate-duty proceeding concerning a gift, if the donee did not immediately assume exclusive possession or did not thereafter retain it to the donor’s exclusion, the gifted property is treated as passing on the donor’s death.

issues.legal_issue: The phrase “by contract or otherwise” concerns a legally enforceable obligation or transaction conferring a benefit on the donor, but does not qualify the separate requirement that the donor be excluded from the property itself.
material_facts: The appellant argued that “otherwise” should be read ejusdem generis with “contract.”
The donor continued to reside in the gifted house, although no enforceable arrangement gave him a right to reside there.
issues.conclusion: “Otherwise” refers to a legal obligation or transaction enforceable at law or in equity that confers a benefit on the donor; that phrase does not require an enforceable arrangement for the donor’s continued possession of the property itself.
issues.legal_principle: In the second limb of section 10 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953, “otherwise” is construed ejusdem generis with “contract” to cover a legal obligation or transaction enforceable at law or in equity that confers a benefit on the donor. The second limb does not control the separate first-limb requirement of exclusion from the property. The Court considered Attorney-General v. Seccombe on the meaning of “otherwise,” but relied on Chick v. Commissioner of Stamp Duties of New South Wales and Commissioner of Stamp Duties of New South Wales v. Owens in addressing exclusion from the property.

predicates.estate_duty_gift_proceeding: The matter is an estate-duty proceeding concerning property transferred by gift.
predicates.otherwise_refers_to_an_enforceable_legal: The phrase concerning benefits to the donor covers enforceable legal arrangements conferring such a benefit and does not limit the separate requirement that the donor be excluded from the property.

issues.definition: In an estate-duty gift proceeding, the phrase concerning other benefits to the donor covers enforceable legal arrangements and does not qualify the separate property-exclusion requirement.

issues.legal_issue: A later prospective amendment to the gift-related estate-duty rule does not govern an earlier transfer or retrospectively alter the rule applicable to it.
material_facts: The gift and the donor’s death occurred before the amendment relied on by the appellant came into force.
The amendment provided that residence in a gifted house by specified close relatives would not, by itself, cause the house to be deemed to pass, subject to stated qualifications.
The amendment was made effective prospectively.
issues.conclusion: The appellant could not rely on the later amendment to determine the estate-duty treatment of the earlier gift.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the amendment made by the Finance Act, 1965, which inserted a further proviso into section 10 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953, was effective prospectively and was not retrospective. It therefore did not govern the earlier gift. The Court declined to use the later amendment as an interpretive basis for changing the meaning of the earlier provision.

predicates.estate_duty_gift_proceeding: The matter is an estate-duty proceeding concerning property transferred by gift.
predicates.transfer_preceded_amendment: The property transfer occurred before a later amendment to the governing rule came into effect.
predicates.amendment_is_prospective: The later amendment was made effective prospectively rather than retrospectively.
predicates.later_amendment_does_not_retroactively_g: The later amendment does not determine the treatment of the earlier transfer.

issues.definition: When a gift in an estate-duty proceeding preceded a prospective amendment, the amendment does not govern that earlier transfer.

issues.legal_issue: Property registered jointly in the names of spouses may be included in full in the deceased spouse’s estate where the deceased supplied the purchase funds and the other spouse was only a name-lender.
material_facts: The house stood in the joint names of the deceased and his wife.

The Board found that the property had been purchased entirely with the deceased’s funds, that he had declared the entire property as his own for income-tax purposes, and that its income had been assessed exclusively in his hands.
The Board found that the wife was merely a name-lender and that the entire property belonged to the deceased.
issues.conclusion: The entire property, rather than only a half share, was properly included in the deceased’s estate for estate-duty assessment.
issues.legal_principle: The Court accepted the Board’s factual finding that the deceased owned the entire property despite joint registration, because he had supplied all the purchase funds and treated the whole property and its income as his own. On that finding, the appellant could not limit the estate-duty assessment to half the property under sections 5 and 10 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953.

rule.if: estate_duty_assessment_proceeding and property_is_jointly_registered and deceased_supplied_all_purchase_funds and other_registered_owner_was_only_a_name_lender

predicates.estate_duty_assessment_proceeding: The matter is an assessment of estate duty on a deceased person’s estate.
predicates.property_is_jointly_registered: The property is registered in the names of the deceased and another person.
predicates.deceased_supplied_all_purchase_funds: The deceased supplied all the funds used to purchase the property.
predicates.other_registered_owner_was_only_a_name_l: The other registered owner held title in name only and had no beneficial ownership of the property.
predicates.entire_property_is_included_in_deceased_: The whole property, rather than only a share, is included in the deceased’s estate for assessment.

issues.definition: In an estate-duty assessment, if jointly registered property was wholly funded by the deceased and the other registered owner was only a name-lender, the whole property is included in the deceased’s estate.
